title: Whitman's Leaves of Grass
objective: After this level you can explain how Whitman's long free-verse lines tried to hold all of America.
summary: Whitman self-published twelve untitled poems in 1855. His 'I' grows to hold every reader, his long free-verse catalogs list working Americans, and he kept expanding the book until he died.

cards.headline: In 1855 a Brooklyn printer published a book of twelve untitled poems.
cards.body: Walt Whitman had worked in Brooklyn as a printer and newspaper journalist. The first Leaves of Grass was a slim book he published himself: twelve poems with no titles, plus a preface. Inside was a voice that wanted to hold an entire country.

cards.headline: "I" means you too
cards.body: The poem later famous as "Song of Myself" opens: "I celebrate myself, and sing myself, / And what I assume you shall assume, / For every atom belonging to me as good belongs to you." Whitman's "myself" keeps swelling until it takes in the reader, then everyone. Caught contradicting himself, he shrugs: "Very well then I contradict myself, / (I am large, I contain multitudes.)"

cards.headline: A list as long as a country
cards.body: One of Whitman's great tools is the list. In "I Hear America Singing" come the mechanics, the carpenter, the mason, the boatman, the shoemaker, "Each singing what belongs to him or her and to none else". The lines run long, with no rhyme and no regular beat: what the National Park Service calls "a free-verse avalanche". A country that big needed a line that long.

cards.fact: Whitman spent the rest of his life rewriting one book.
cards.context: He kept refining Leaves of Grass through edition after edition. The second, in 1856, already had thirty-two poems. The last, the "deathbed edition" of 1891-92, was still getting additions when he died in 1892. Like the singers of Homer's tradition, who reshaped inherited poems in every performance, Whitman never treated his book as finished.
